pl-l2d43c1-d1e108.summary: Introduces a kind of sin graver and more abominable than others, the sin against the Holy Spirit: whoever sins against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven here or hereafter (Matt 12:32); John says there is a sin unto death for which he does not say to pray; sin against Father or Son is forgiven, blasphemy against the Spirit is not.
claims: The sin against the Holy Spirit is unforgiven.

pl-l2d43c1-d1e111.summary: Asks what the sin against the Holy Spirit or unto death is.

pl-l2d43c1-d1e114.summary: Reports some who say it is despair or obstinacy: obstinacy is the pertinacity of a mind hardened in malice, making one impenitent; despair is wholly distrusting God's goodness, thinking one's malice exceeds it, like Cain. Both are against the Spirit, the love and boundless goodness of Father and Son: the obstinate abuse God's patience and presume on mercy, thinking God not just; the despairing think him not good, removing the harbor of divine pardon and adding sins to sins.
claims: Despair and obstinacy offend the Spirit's goodness.

pl-l2d43c1-d1e120.summary: Asks whether every obstinacy of a hardened mind and every despair is the sin against the Holy Spirit.

pl-l2d43c1-d1e123.summary: Reports some who say yes; then the sin is sometimes forgiven, since many most obstinate and desperate are converted, as Augustine shows on the Psalms (turning into the depth of the sea; sending crystal like morsels of bread, making the obstinate teachers of others). On this view it is called irremissible because forgiven rarely and with difficulty, as crystal is dissolved only by a strong wind.
claims: On one view it is rarely, not never, forgiven.

pl-l2d43c1-d1e126.summary: Reports others who say only obstinacy or despair accompanied by impenitence is the sin, citing Augustine that impenitence is the sin against the Holy Spirit; on this view it is never forgiven, as Augustine says it alone cannot merit pardon and Jerome that such a sinner cannot worthily repent; so John says not to pray for it, since such a one, with a heart hardened like the devil's, cannot be helped by the Church's prayers here or hereafter.
claims: On another view it is never forgiven, being joined to impenitence.

pl-l2d43c1-d1e131.summary: Gives another account from De sermone Domini: sin unto death is when, after knowing God through Christ's grace, one attacks the brotherhood and is driven by envy against the grace by which he was reconciled; perhaps this is sinning against the Spirit, unforgiven not because pardon is refused the penitent but because its stain prevents the humility of asking, as Judas, saying 'I have sinned,' ran to the noose rather than seek pardon.
claims: The sin is envious attack on grace and brotherhood.

pl-l2d43c1-d1e134.summary: Notes this account makes the sin an attack on brotherhood after knowledge and envy of grace after reconciliation, which can be understood as a species of obstinacy.
claims: It is a species of obstinacy.

pl-l2d43c1-d1e137.summary: Cites the Retractationes: Augustine did not assert this but said he thought it, and should have added 'if he ends this life in that wicked perversity,' since no one in this life is to be despaired of, and prayer for one not despaired of is not imprudent.
claims: The sin holds only if one dies in it.

pl-l2d43c1-d1e141.summary: Concludes that the sin so described is unto death only when penance does not accompany it; no sinner in this life is to be despaired of, so we must pray for all; John's 'I do not say to pray for it' means not praying for one who sinned unto death after he has ended this life.
claims: Pray for every living sinner.

pl-l2d43c1-d1e144.summary: Cites Augustine, De verbis Domini, on impenitence as blasphemy against the Spirit: it cannot be judged while one lives, since God's patience leads to penance; one who is pagan, Jew, heretic, or schismatic today may embrace Catholic peace tomorrow; do not judge before the time.
claims: Impenitence cannot be judged in this life.

pl-l2d43c1-d1e147.summary: Concludes that we must pray for every sinner in this life, distrusting none, since one can be converted while living, and it cannot be known whether someone sinned unto death until he leaves this life, unless revealed by the Spirit.
claims: Final impenitence is known only after death.

pl-l2d43c1-d1e150.summary: Summarizes that the sin against the Spirit is envy of grace attacking the brotherhood impenitently, which seems to be obstinacy, and every obstinacy and despair of the impenitent. Not everyone who does not repent is impenitent, since impenitence properly belongs to the obstinate, and some say also the despairing.
claims: Impenitence belongs to the obstinate and despairing.

pl-l2d43c1-d1e153.summary: Cites Ambrose, De Spiritu sancto: there is not one offense against the Son and another against the Spirit, for as dignity is one, so is injury; one deceived by Christ's human form who thinks less of his flesh than is fitting has fault but is not excluded from pardon; but one who denies the Spirit's eternal dignity, majesty, and power and thinks demons cast out by Beelzebub cannot be pardoned, since there is fullness of sacrilege.
claims: Denying the Spirit's work as Beelzebub's is unforgivable.

pl-l2d43c1-d1e158.summary: Notes this agrees with Augustine's description as envy of grace attacking the brotherhood, since one who after knowing the truth denies the Spirit's truth and attributes his works to Beelzebub envies God's power, goodness, and grace.
claims: Ambrose and Augustine agree.

pl-l2d43c1-d1e162.summary: Explains that the distinction does not divide offenses among three persons but distinguishes kinds of sin: against the Father, by weakness, since power is often attributed to the Father; against the Son, by ignorance, since wisdom is attributed to the Son; the third has been explained. Sins of weakness or ignorance easily obtain pardon, but not sin against the Spirit. Why power, wisdom, and goodness, one in the three, are assigned to the persons was said earlier.
claims: Sins against Father, Son, and Spirit are sins of weakness, ignorance, and malice.

pl-l2d43c1.summary: Treats the sin against the Holy Spirit, graver than others and unforgiven here or hereafter (Matt 12:32; 1 John 5:16). Some identify it with despair, distrusting God's goodness like Cain, and obstinacy, the pertinacity of a mind hardened in malice that leads to impenitence; both offend the Spirit, the love and goodness of Father and Son. Some say every obstinacy and despair is this sin, called irremissible because rarely and with difficulty forgiven; others say only those joined to impenitence, so it is never forgiven, and John forbids praying for it. Augustine also defined it as attacking the brotherhood and envying grace after knowing God, but in the Retractationes added 'if one ends this life in it'; so no one in this life is to be despaired of, and we must pray for all, since whether someone sinned against the Spirit is known only after death. Ambrose: it is denying the Spirit's eternal majesty and attributing his works to Beelzebub. The distinction of sins against Father, Son, and Spirit is not of offenses against divided persons but of kinds: against the Father by weakness, the Son by ignorance, the Spirit by malice, according to the appropriated attributes of power, wisdom, and goodness.
claims: The sin against the Holy Spirit is unforgiven here or hereafter.
Some identify it with despair and obstinacy.
It offends the Holy Spirit, who is the goodness and love of Father and Son.
Some hold it is irremissible because rarely forgiven; others because never forgiven, being joined to impenitence.
Augustine defined it as envious attack on grace and brotherhood after knowing God, if one dies in it.
No one in this life is to be despaired of, and we must pray for all sinners.
Sins against Father, Son, and Spirit are sins of weakness, ignorance, and malice, by appropriation.
